clue.text: Man with Mrs Gore, embracing her, surely wasn't 8

parts.note: Jack is a generic name for a man, as in every man jack

indicators.note: the wife's name wraps round the following word, holding it inside

parts.note: Tipper Gore is the wife of the US vice-president Al Gore
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man in Mrs Gore's company, with his arm round her, can't possibly have been the man at 8.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on 8 down: Walter Sickert is a painter whom some writers, notably Patricia Cornwell, have named as the Victorian Whitechapel murderer, a claim Araucaria doubts. Tipper Gore is Al Gore's wife.
explanation.definitionFit: The Whitechapel murderer has been identified by some with the painter at 8 down; the setter's definition asserts that identification is false.

clue.text: Separate people after a time in the living room

indicators.note: the time letter is placed after the other pieces

parts.note: separate as an adverb means apart
men are people
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone splits people off a while later in the lounge.
explanation.definitionFit: An apartment can mean a single room in a house, here one lived in.

clue.text: Ringer for dead king and girlfriend?

parts.note: K is the chess and cards abbreviation for king
Nell Gwyn was the mistress of Charles II, so the dead king's girlfriend is Nell

explanation.surface: Who tolled the bell for the late monarch and his lady friend?
explanation.walkthrough: The dead king of the surface is Charles II, whose famous mistress was the actress Nell Gwyn.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers allows a ringer to be something that rings, and a funeral bell's toll sounds for the departed.

clue.text: Handy sort of musician

indicators.note: a sort of handy thing is a version of it, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A musician who is good with his hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' reworks the letters of HANDY.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Haydn was the Austrian composer of the Classical period, a famous example of a musician.

clue.text: Hurry to desert visitor to Mansfield Park

parts.note: to hurry is to rush
one's desert, what one deserves, is one's worth or merit

explanation.surface: Someone hastens to abandon a guest at the Bertrams' country house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'desert' is not the verb to abandon but the noun as in 'just deserts'. Mansfield Park is Jane Austen's novel, in which Mr Rushworth calls as suitor to Maria Bertram.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Rushworth is the wealthy suitor in Austen's novel who calls at the Bertram family home.

clue.text: Lubricator of too much in France put up a case for a minister

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting the phrase up reads it from bottom to top

parts.note: oil is a lubricator
taken as written
trop is French for too much

explanation.surface: Someone raises a container of oil to excess, French-style, for a government official.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' turns the whole phrase OIL OF TROP backwards from the bottom of the down light.
explanation.definitionFit: A portfolio is the case for carrying papers, and by extension a minister's department.

clue.text: In this context rationality is a plus

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of letters of the two following words

explanation.surface: Being rational in this setting counts in one's favour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' shows the answer lies within contEXT RAtionality.
explanation.definitionFit: An extra is something added on, a bonus or additional item.

clue.text: Painter has to change being less healthy in weight

indicators.note: the change and the sicker state go inside the weight abbreviation

parts.note: to change is to alter
sicker means less healthy

explanation.surface: An artist must alter, growing more ill as he gains pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' and 'being' are link words; 'weight' is the container, not part of the painter's health.
explanation.definitionFit: Walter Sickert was a British painter of the Camden Town Group, sometimes named as a Ripper suspect.

clue.text: Ban on pictures by Hogarth — two works destroyed in New York

indicators.note: the shuffled letters are placed in the abbreviation for the city

parts.note: op, short for opus, is a musical work

indicators.note: something destroyed is broken up, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the second of the two works is another op

explanation.surface: Prints by Hogarth are barred after two of his pieces are wrecked in Manhattan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'destroyed' rearranges HOGARTH with one OP into HOTOGRAPH; the other OP leads, and the whole goes 'in' NY. Hogarth was an engraver, so 'pictures by Hogarth' sounds natural.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-photography notice bans the taking of pictures, as in museums.

clue.text: A rebel at the setter's school

parts.note: Jack Cade led a rebellion in Kent in 1450
the setter's is my, from the setter's own point of view

explanation.surface: A rebel turns up at the crossword compiler's place of learning.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Cade is the leader of the 1450 Kentish revolt, a stock crossword rebel; 'the setter' refers to the compiler, so 'the setter's' becomes MY.
explanation.definitionFit: An academy is a school or place of training.

clue.text: Nameless town with church music extract

indicators.note: N is the abbreviation for name, so a nameless word loses that letter

parts.note: Church Stretton is a town in Shropshire, so Stretton is the town that goes with Church

explanation.surface: A small town without a name has a church and a snatch of music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with church' is not a link: the town is Church Stretton, a Shropshire town, so the clue gives STRETTON, and 'Nameless' takes away its N.
explanation.definitionFit: A stretto is a passage in a fugue where the entries of the subject overlap, a section of a musical piece.

clue.text: Destroy nearly everything after a drink

indicators.note: the shortened word is placed after the drink

parts.note: a tot is a small drink of spirits

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all of the word, so its last letter goes

parts.note: everything means all

explanation.surface: Someone wrecks almost the whole lot after a nip of whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'total' a car is to wreck it beyond repair, so 'Destroy' works as a verb definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To total a car is a slang way to write it off, to wreck it completely.

clue.text: "Fluid found in garment just bought"(preliminary bulletin)

parts.note: something just bought is new

indicators.note: the fluid abbreviation is placed in the garment

parts.note: a sash is a garment worn round the waist or over the shoulder
FL is the abbreviation for fluid, as in fl oz

explanation.surface: A headline about liquid discovered in brand-new clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is set out as a quoted headline followed by the definition in brackets; 'just bought' gives the first part of the answer although it is printed last.
explanation.definitionFit: A newsflash is a brief early report of breaking news, given ahead of full coverage.

clue.text: Woman pursuing engineer officer

indicators.note: the woman follows the engineer, coming after it

parts.note: RE stands for the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
Eve is the first woman

explanation.surface: A woman chasing a military engineer.
explanation.walkthrough: RE, the Royal Engineers, is the usual crossword engineer; the woman is the biblical first woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A reeve was a local official or magistrate in medieval England.

clue.text: Powerful stuff offset with circle

indicators.note: off means awry or out of place, so the letters of set and circle are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something mighty is balanced by a ring.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'offset' is split in two: its first three letters are the anagram signal and its last three are fodder, a loose but playful trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Electrics are the electrical fittings of a house or car, the gear that carries power.

clue.text: Maybe Mr Goethe left one not his last letter, his last words

indicators.note: maybe suggests a possible version of the words, so the letters are rearranged
the final letter of the poet's name is left off

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Perhaps Herr Goethe left something out of his final letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not his last letter' cuts GOETHE to GOETH; with MR, L and I that is rearranged by 'Maybe'. Goethe's reported dying words were 'Mehr Licht'.
explanation.definitionFit: Goethe's last words are traditionally reported in English as a call for more light.

clue.text: We made our version of a wild flower

indicators.note: a version of the words is a reworking, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: We produced our own account of a meadow plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'version of' rearranges WE MADE OUR.
explanation.definitionFit: Meadow rue is a wild plant of the buttercup family with fluffy flowers.

clue.text: Brown coal placed under earth is explosive

indicators.note: in a down entry, the coal comes below the earth

parts.note: Ge or Gaia is the Greek goddess of the earth
lignite is soft brown coal

explanation.surface: Brown coal buried beneath the ground can blow up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'placed under' puts LIGNITE below GE in the down light.
explanation.definitionFit: Gelignite is a blasting explosive made with nitroglycerine.

clue.text: Where things (such as flowers in Beds) come out

definitions.text: Where things (such as flowers in Beds) come out

parts.words: Where things (such as flowers in Beds) come out
parts.note: a problem is said to come out at laundering time; a flower is a river, and Bedfordshire's Great Ouse comes out into a bay of the North Sea

explanation.surface: Where garden flowers emerge in their beds.
explanation.walkthrough: Beds is short for Bedfordshire, an English county, and 'flowers' are rivers; the Great Ouse flows through it to the bay on the Lincolnshire and Norfolk coast. 'Come out in the ...' is an idiom for problems resolving.
explanation.definitionFit: Things come out in the laundering, the idiom for difficulties resolving themselves; also where Bedfordshire's rivers reach the sea.

clue.text: Prisoner's camp

parts.note: the possessive reads as 'of' a prisoner
a lag is a convict, a prisoner

explanation.surface: A camp holding captives.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive 'Prisoner's' is read as OF LAG, 'of a convict'; an Oflag was a German prisoner-of-war camp for officers.
explanation.definitionFit: An Oflag was a Second World War German prison camp for captured officers.

clue.text: One go at typing crucial transactions in Peterborough

parts.note: crucial means key, of vital importance

indicators.note: the abbreviation for transactions is placed inside the district

parts.note: the Soke of Peterborough was an old administrative district of England
TR or trans is an abbreviation for transactions, as in learned society proceedings

explanation.surface: A single attempt at typing important dealings in a Cambridgeshire city.
explanation.walkthrough: The Soke of Peterborough was a historic administrative district round that English city, now in Cambridgeshire.
explanation.definitionFit: A keystroke is one press of a key on a keyboard, a single go at typing.

clue.text: Greeting of French student with Swiss voice?

parts.note: yo is an informal greeting
de is French for of
L is for learner, the student driver's plate

explanation.surface: A hello from a French pupil with a Swiss accent.
explanation.walkthrough: L comes from the learner plates on a student driver's car.
explanation.definitionFit: Yodelling is the warbling singing style of Alpine Switzerland, hence the question mark for a Swiss voice.

clue.text: Take in about 10p from one far from home

indicators.note: the eating goes round the coin, enclosing it

parts.note: to take in food is to eat
X is the Roman numeral for ten, with P for pence

explanation.surface: Someone abroad accepts roughly ten pence.
explanation.walkthrough: '10p' reads as ten pence but here is the Roman numeral plus the pence abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: An expat, short for expatriate, lives outside their native country.

clue.text: Pursue graduate for settled teaching

parts.note: to dog someone is to follow them doggedly
an MA, Master of Arts, is a graduate

explanation.surface: Chase a degree holder for established instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Dogma is an established, authoritative body of doctrine.

clue.text: Fancy starting again inside mummy?

indicators.note: the prefix for again goes inside the mother

parts.note: a dam is an animal mother
re is a prefix meaning again

explanation.surface: Imagining things are starting up again within an Egyptian mummy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starting' is a link; 'mummy' is not the Egyptian kind but a mother, a dam; 'inside' puts RE in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Fancy and dream both mean an imagined wish or fantasy.

clue.text: Director grabs one like nymph compared with cherry

indicators.note: the steering device takes hold of the numeral, enclosing it

parts.note: a rudder directs a ship
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A director seizes one, like a nymph beside a cherry.
explanation.walkthrough: From Handel's Acis and Galatea: 'O ruddier than the cherry' is sung of the nymph Galatea.
explanation.definitionFit: The giant in Handel's opera sings that the nymph Galatea is redder than the cherry.

clue.text: Fairly bicoloured kitchen object

parts.note: pied means patched in two colours, like a magpie
-ish means fairly or somewhat

explanation.surface: A rather two-toned item from the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: PIED comes first in the answer although 'bicoloured' is printed second.
explanation.definitionFit: A pie dish is a baking dish found in the kitchen.

clue.text: Silencers add lustre to city with heartless soldiers

parts.note: to gloss is to add shine or lustre
EC is the postcode for the City of London

indicators.note: the middle letter of the word is removed

parts.note: Tommies are British soldiers

explanation.surface: Gun mufflers polish up the town with gutless troops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' drops the central M of TOMMIES; EC is the City of London postcode.
explanation.definitionFit: Glossectomy is the surgical removal of the tongue, which would silence a person.
